Article https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-64650-1 How augmin establishes the angle of the microtubule branch site

Sophie M. Travis1,4,6, Jodi Kraus1,6, Collin T. McManus 1,5, Kiana Golden 2, Rui Zhang 3 & Sabine Petry 1

How microtubules (MTs) are generated in the proper orientation is essential to understanding how the cytoskeleton organizes a cell and MT-dependent events such as cell division. In the spindle, most MTs are generated through the branching MT nucleation pathway. In this pathway, new MTs are nucleated from the side of existing MTs and oriented at a shallow angle by the branching factor augmin, ensuring that both MTs have the same polarity. Yet, how augmin binds MTs and sets the branch angle has remained unclear. Here, we report the cryo-electron microscopy structure of an augmin subcomplex on the MT. This structure resembles that of NDC80 bound to the MT, with the conserved CH domain of augmin’s Haus6 subunit directly proximal to the MT lattice. We ﬁnd that the Haus6 CH domain is a bona ﬁde MT binding site that increases augmin’s afﬁnity for the MT and helps establish branch angle. A second binding site, located in the disordered N-terminus of Haus8, also establishes branch angle,. Thus, we ﬁnd that augmin regulates MT branching using two domains, each tuned to modulate MT afﬁnity and MT branch angle. This work expands our mechanistic understanding of branching MT nucleation and thus spindle formation.

Microtubules (MTs) are a primary component of the eukaryotic cytoskeleton, where they play critical roles in organellar and vesicular trafﬁcking, cellular motility, and, during cell division, chromosome segregation. For each of these roles, new MTs must be generated on demand in real-time through MT nucleation. Moreover, the polarity of new MTs must be strictly controlled to ensure that cargos and chromosomes are correctly trafﬁcked. MT nucleation proceeds through multiple biochemical pathways, and one of the most important during spindle assembly is branching MT nucleation1–4. New branched daughter MTs emanate at a shallow angle, generally between 0° and 30°, and share the same polarity of the pre-existing mother MTs5,6. Thus, on the micron scale, branching MT nucleation preserves spindle MT polarity. Several MT-associated proteins (MAPs) have been shown to promote branching MT nucleation6–8. However, in its simplest form,

branching MT nucleation requires only two protein complexes: the universal MT nucleator γ-TuRC and the branching-speciﬁc heterooctameric augmin complex9–11. Augmin’s primary function in branching MT nucleation is to recruit γ-TuRC to pre-existing MTs12,13. Moreover, augmin appears to establish the overall architecture of the MT branch site, as reconstitution of MT branching with only augmin and γ- TuRC recapitulates the shallow branch angles observed in endogenous branching9–11,14. Yet, how augmin orients γ-TuRC and the daughter MT of the resulting branch has remained unclear. Recent experimental models of both human and Xenopus laevis augmin, determined using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (EM), have provided the groundwork to answer this question14–16. These models demonstrated that augmin is a relatively rigid complex, composed of a γ-TuRC-binding stalk (T-III) and an arch (T-II) that binds the pre-existing MT12,13,17. thus made the complex seem a good candidate to enforce a deﬁned range of angles between γ-TuRC and the pre-existing MT, one major issue remained. Prior biochemical data had implicated the N-terminus of T-II subunit Haus8, a low-complexity, highly electropositive 150- residue sequence, as the primary MT binding region (MTBR) within the complex12,18. Yet, no electron density corresponding to this region could be found in any of the experimental datasets, presumably due to inherent ﬂexibility14–16. This begs the question: if augmin connects to the pre-existing MT only via a ﬂexible, unstructured region, how can augmin possibly impose global structure on the branch site and deﬁne the range of branch angles. To answer this question, in this work, we report the cryo-electron microscopy structure of an augmin subcomplex bound to the MT lattice. Our prior structures had found that augmin contains two CH domains, which are often MT binding regions. The structure of augmin on the MT reveals that the CH domain of Haus6 is, in fact, a bona ﬁde MT binding region. Using structure-based biochemistry, we characterize the role of the MT binding regions and uncover how augmin regulates MT binding and branching angle, which is important for its function in the spindle during cell division.

Results Engineering augmin T-IIbonsai To understand how augmin interacts with the lattice of the mother MT, we needed to obtain the structure of augmin bound to the MT. Prior work from our lab and others12,13 established that full-length augmin can be visualized sparsely decorating MTs. However, it was not possible to produce full-length augmin above the dissociation constant of 1 μM previously reported12, making it infeasible to saturate the MT lattice with full-length augmin, as would be required for single particle cryo-EM. Thus, we explored truncations of the augmin complex, as well as subcomplexes, to identify a more tractable structural target. Our prior structure of X. laevis augmin14 suggested that both the MTBR of Haus8, as well as the putative MT-binding CH domains of Haus6 and Haus7 were clustered at the N-terminus of tetramer T-II (Fig. 1a). Using the augmin structure as a guide, we located an internal hinge at the apex of T-II (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1a, b). We truncated T-II at this hinge and were able to produce a shortened T-II that we termed augmin T-IIbonsai (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1a, b). Surprisingly, Haus2 was excluded from the complex upon puriﬁcation (Supplementary Fig. 1c). This is consistent with the more transient association of Haus2 with T-II that we had previously reported13. Nonetheless, the Haus6/Haus7/Haus8 heterotrimeric subcomplex was predicted to still form a folded, albeit remodeled, heterotrimer that, crucially, maintains the same architecture of the MT-binding regions as the full-length complex (Supplementary Fig. 1d). Furthermore, the complex was highly soluble and could be produced at a concentration of 10 μM. Using MT pelleting assays, we determined the afﬁnity of T-IIbonsai for the MT lattice as 200 ± 80 nM (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b), in line with the previously reported afﬁnity of the full length complex12. Thus, we established that T-IIbonsai was a promising target for structural studies on the MT lattice.

Structure of augmin T-IIbonsai on the MT To determine the structure of augmin T-IIbonsai bound to the MT lattice, we prepared grids of GMPCPP-stabilized MTs, then ﬂowed in the augmin T-IIbonsai construct before grid blotting and freezing. After screening for coated MTs (Supplementary Fig. 6), data collection (Supplementary Table 1), and data processing (Supplementary Fig. 6), we obtained a reconstruction of the 14-protoﬁlament GMPCPP-stabilized MT decorated with density corresponding to T-IIbonsai at 3.8 Å resolution (Fig. 1b, Supplementary Fig. 6). Symmetry expansion followed by further reﬁnement led to a reconstruction of a single tubulin dimer bound to a single copy of T-IIbonsai at 3.1 Å resolution (Fig. 1c). The highest resolution region of the map corresponded to the MT

lattice (Supplementary Fig. 7a, b), however, the resolution of the T-IIbonsai density, ranging from 3 to 5 Å, was sufﬁcient to interpret the structure of T-IIbonsai bound to the MT. Although in the full augmin structure, T-IIbonsai forms a rigid unit, in our structure, only a portion of the T-IIbonsai is visible. This portion consists of a single CH domain, closest to the MT lattice, and an adjacent stalk region, composed of three α-helices, that points away from the lattice (Fig. 1d). This stalk is the precise length of the α-helical trimer at the N-terminus of T-II prior to incorporation of the Haus2 α- helix into a tetrameric bundle (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Thus, we may observe ordered density for only a portion of the complex because, in the absence of Haus2, the remainder fails to fold. Rigid-body docking of the N-terminus of T-II into the density was most consistent with Haus6 contributing the ordered CH domain, rather than Haus7, as this allowed for correct positioning of the α-helical stalk (Supplementary Fig. 8a, b). Furthermore, docking of the predicted structure of the Haus6 CH domain appropriately positions many bulky aromatic residues within the density (Supplementary Fig. 8c, d). These bulky residues are generally not conserved between Haus6 and Haus7 (Supplementary Fig. 8e), so this provides further agreement with our assignment of the Haus6 CH domain as closest to the MT lattice. Our structure shows a modest binding surface between augmin and the MT lattice (Fig. 2a), with a buried surface area of 664 Å2. A little under half of the binding surface (309 Å2) contacts α-tubulin, mediated by αB’ and αE loop of Haus6 (Fig. 2a, Supplementary Fig. 9a). In addition, the short αF helix of Haus6, although down weighted by the deep-learning driven sharpening algorithm deepEMhancer, is visible in close proximity to β-tubulin in traditionally, globally-sharpened map (Supplementary Fig. 9b, c), and contributes an additional 355 Å2 of buried surface area. In addition to the CH domain of Haus6, augmin has been proposed to contain two other MT binding sites: the CH domain of Haus716

and the MTBR of Haus812,18 As discussed above, the CH domain of Haus7 is not visible in our structure; however, its position can be inferred by docking larger fragments of augmin into our map (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Thus, our structure implies that the Haus7 CH domain may not directly contact the MT lattice. Surprisingly, we observe no additional density in our map that could correspond to the Haus8 N-terminal MTBR (Supplementary Fig. 10a, b). As the highly electronegative tails of α- and β-tubulin are predicted to be adjacent to the location to the Haus8 MTBR (Fig. 2a), we speculate that Haus8’s N-terminal electropositive MTBR may contribute to electrostatic attraction to the tubulin tails, thus enhancing augmin’s MT binding afﬁnity without displaying appreciable ordered binding. Previous studies have shown that augmin shows substantial afﬁnity for the tubulin tails19, and similar phenomena have been previously reported for regions of many electropositive MAPs, such as tau20 and NDC8021,22.

Roles of the bipartite binding interface in MT binding afﬁnity From our structure, the Haus6 CH domain appears to be wellpositioned to interact with the tubulin lattice (Fig. 2a). Moreover, the surface adjacent to the tubulin dimer is both conserved and electropositive (Fig. 2b). Thus, we hypothesized that the Haus6 CH domain could contribute to augmin’s MT binding afﬁnity. We tested this hypothesis by assessing which regions of augmin are necessary for MT binding. We generated augmin mutants that were missing the Haus8 MTBR or the Haus6 CH domain, as well as a mutant missing the Haus7 CH domain. Next, we visualized the binding of augmin mutants to immobilized, ﬂuorescently labeled GMPCPP MT seeds via total internal reﬂection (TIRF) microscopy. As expected, wildtype augmin displayed robust binding to the MT seeds (Fig. 2c). Previous work using human augmin suggested that deletion of the Haus8 MTBR was sufﬁcient to abrogate MT binding of the entire complex12. However, when we deleted the Haus8 MTBR from X. laevis augmin, we found that MT binding was weakened but not abolished (Fig. 2c, d). Similarly, puriﬁed

MT lattice preference of branching factors As described above, T-II and NDC80 have marked structural and biochemical similarities in how the complexes bind to MTs. Yet, one major difference between the two complexes is their localization on the MT. The NDC80 complex, in its role of capturing MT plus ends at the kinetochore, prefers and tracks the lattice at the growing MT plus end23. In contrast, augmin tends to localize along the entire MT and enable branching MT nucleation uniformly along its length. Moreover, augmin has not been reported to have any plus-end tracking activity, either in vitro, in X. laevis egg extract, or in vivo. Therefore, we investigated whether augmin’s localization could be explained by a preference for a speciﬁc nucleotide state of the MT lattice. To directly investigate augmin’s lattice preference, we employed two variations on a dual-lattice TIRF microscopy binding assay, inspired by Mauer et al. and Zhang et al. 28,29. In the ﬁrst variation, we initially nucleated Atto 647N-labeled GMPCPP MT seeds, then performed another round of polymerization with Alexa568 tubulin and GTPγS. The resulting MTs had regions that mimic the GTP MT lattice (GMPCPP), at the plus end, and the GDP + Pi transition state (GTPγS), further from the plus end, each labeled with a distinct ﬂuorophore. As a proof of concept, we incubated seeds with EB1 and found, as previously reported, that the protein preferred the GTPγS lattice over GMPCPP (Fig. 3a, b, Supplementary Fig. 13)26,29. The branching factor TPX2 has been previously reported to prefer GMPCPP lattice30, and we also recapitulated this preference for the GMPCPP lattice (Fig. 3a, b, Supplementary Fig. 13). Having shown that proteins can preferentially localize to both lattice types in our system, we next assayed augmin’s lattice preference. We found that augmin, like EB1, strongly prefers the GTPγS lattice over GMPCPP (Fig. 3a, b), suggesting that, consistent with prior observations, augmin does not preferentially bind lattice found at the plus-end11,31. In addition, augmin lacking the MTBR of Haus8 maintains its preference for GTPγS lattice over GMPCPP, suggesting that lattice preference is encoded in the Haus6 CH domain (Fig. 3a, b). Prior experiments using dynamic MTs found preferential accumulation of augmin and other branching factors on older lattice. This could be due to slow kinetics of augmin accumulation or, alternatively, a preference for GDP lattice. Thus, we next asked whether augmin displayed any preference for GDP lattice over the other types. To address this question, we modiﬁed our lattice preference conditions by mixing the above-described GMPCPP-GTPγS MTs with orthogonally-colored dynamic MTs—presumed to be fully converted to GDP lattice—capped by GMPCPP for stability. Using this modiﬁed set-up, we ﬁnd that, as previously reported, EB1 preferentially binds the GTPγS lattice over the GDP lattice (Fig. 3c, d). Under our assay conditions, TPX2 displays a minor but signiﬁcant preference for GTPγS over GDP. In addition, we observe that augmin displays a minor but statistically signiﬁcant preferential localization to the GTPγS over GDP lattice (Fig. 3c, d). Taking all this data together, we ﬁnd that augmin’s primary preference is for more native, compacted lattice instead of the expanded GMPCPP lattice. Additionally, augmin displays a slight preference for GTPγS lattice over GDP lattice, although this preference is less pronounced than the preference for GTPγS over GMPCPP. To conﬁrm that lattice mismatch did not cause distortions to the structure of augmin on the MT, we solved a moderate-resolution structure of T-IIbonsai bound to the GTPγS lattice (Supplementary Figs. 14–16, Supplementary Table 1). At this resolution, approximately

8 Å around augmin (Supplementary Figs. 12d, 16a), we can resolve secondary structure corresponding to T-IIbonsai. We ﬁnd that Haus6’s CH domain directly contacts the GTPγS lattice in a similar manner to the GMPCPP lattice (Supplementary Fig. 16b). Compaction of the GTPγS lattice by comparison to GMPCPP, which comprises both interdimer and intradimer compaction as previously reported28, causes a slight reorientation of the Haus6 CH domain. This reorientation, imposed by a minor reorientation of the α11’ helix of α-tubulin, may underlie augmin’s preference for the more biological compacted lattice state, although at the moderate resolution of the GTPγS structure, this cannot be proved conclusively.

In vitro branching reconstitution provides functional implications for the bipartite MT binding region of augmin We and others have previously shown that branching MT nucleation can be reconstituted in vitro using only augmin and γ-TuRC, while still recapitulating the conserved polarity and shallow branch angles observed in X. laevis meiotic egg extract9–11,14. Therefore, we hypothesized that the MT binding sites of augmin contribute to setting the branch angle. To test this, we performed a series of in vitro branching assays from stabilized MT seeds using recombinant augmin. We expressed and puriﬁed wild type augmin as well as octameric augmin constructs lacking either of its MT binding sites, i.e., lacking either the CH domain of Haus6 (Haus6ΔCH) or the N-terminus of Haus8 (Haus8ΔMTBR). To increase the dwell time of augmin on the MT seeds for long enough to observe branching events, we ﬁrst bound BFPtagged full-length TPX2 at a concentration below its phase boundary32. As discussed above, TPX2 strongly binds to the GMPCPP MT lattice. In addition, it is resistant to washout and helps retain augmin on the lattice (Supplementary Fig. 17) long enough to observe branching events for all constructs tested, even the mutants with reduced MT binding. Once augmin was bound to MTs, we incubated the MT seeds with γ-TuRC puriﬁed from X. laevis egg extract. Finally, ﬂuorescently labeled soluble tubulin and GTP were added to initiate branching from the MT seed (Fig. 4, Supplementary Fig. 18, Supplementary Movie 1). As we have shown previously, augmin octamer and γ-TuRC are sufﬁcient to reconstitute branching from MT seeds14. This minimal reaction recapitulates key features of branching, including a shallow branch angle and conservation of overall MT polarity. However, we previously observed branch angles focused around 15–30° for branching performed with augmin octamer14, despite the fact that the most abundant branch angle observed in Xenopus egg extract is 0 to 15 degrees6,31. When we more closely examined the in vitro branching reaction, we found that the most frequent branch angle is in fact between 0 and 15°, due to the presence of previously-overlooked daughter MTs that form parallel (0–5 degrees) to the MT seed. These parallel MTs were observed both through live imaging as well as by an increase in tubulin intensity at the polymerizing MT plus end in later time points. Parallel MTs are easily distinguishable in our live movies of the wildtype augmin octamer, where kymographs of the plus end shows that a new branched MT nucleates at less than 5 degrees alongside the plus end, while the plus end is polymerizing (Supplementary Fig. 19 and Supplementary Movie 7). Additionally, when analyzing still images from different ﬁelds of view at later time points, quantiﬁcation of several MTs at the plus end revealed a mean intensity approximately 2-fold higher than other branched MTs, indicating that a parallel MT existed at the plus end in addition to the one polymerized from the MT seed (Supplementary Fig. 20). This is likely due to the bundling properties of the Haus8 MTBR, as discussed below. We next tested the effect of the augmin Haus8ΔMTBR and Haus6ΔCH constructs on the branching reaction. Despite their decreased afﬁnity for the MT, both constructs are competent to support the nucleation of daughter MTs from the pre-existing seed, (Fig. 4b, Supplementary Movies 2–5). Indeed, by quantifying the average number of branches per seed, we observe an approximately

Follow-up studies will be necessary to fully characterize these ﬂuctuations and determine whether they are con- ﬁned to the minimal reconstituted system or also relevant in the context of the endogenous complement of factors, including motors and other crosslinkers. Nonetheless, our preliminary characterization ﬁnds that, at early timepoints, some individual branches sample a broad range of branch angles, similar in breadth to the range of branch angles found in our bulk sample (Fig. 4e). Some branches are less mobile than others, especially long branches and highly acute branches (with angles <5°). This last is consistent with the idea that acute branches are bundled with the mother MT (Supplementary Fig. 21). To further characterize the role of MT bundling in determining branch angle, we investigated the ability of different augmin constructs to bundle MTs, which had been speculated upon previously18. To test this, we performed an in vitro bundling assay using TIRF microscopy, where we immobilized an Alexa568-MT seed on the glass coverslip and ﬂowed in a solution of augmin and Cy5-MT seeds. Colocalization of augmin with both ﬂuorescently-labeled seeds would indicate augmin is able to bundle the two MTs together, similar to a 0 degree branch angle. We performed this assay with puriﬁed Haus8(1–150), wildtype augmin, and augmin octamer Haus8ΔMTBR construct. In our data, we observe that wildtype augmin can clearly bundle MTs together, and this happens through the MTBR of Haus8 because, when it is deleted, augmin loses its bundling ability (Supplementary Fig. 22).

Discussion In this work, we have reported the cryo-EM structure of an augmin subcomplex, T-IIbonsai, bound to the MT lattice. Surprisingly, this structure displayed no ordered density for the known MT binding N-terminal region of Haus8. Instead, it strongly resembled the structure of NDC80 bound to the MT and revealed a second MT binding site composed of the CH domain of Haus6 in complex with an αβ-tubulin dimer. This interaction between CH domain and MT is critical for augmin to bind the MT with high afﬁnity, as is, to a lesser extent, the Haus8 MTBR. We further found that the augmin complex displays a strong preference for GTPγS-bound MTs over GMPCPP-bound MTs. This spatial preference is the opposite of the strong GMPCPPpreference of the branching factor TPX2. Despite this opposing spatial preference on endogenous-like MTs, we could reconstitute MT branching in vitro using both TPX2 and augmin, along with the MT nucleator γ-TuRC. This allowed us to probe the function of augmin’s two MT binding sites during MT branching. We concluded that both the ordered binding of the Haus6 CH domain, as well as the disordered binding of the Haus8 MTBR, play critical roles in establishing branching geometry and thus in regulating spindle polarity. We were only able to obtain the structure of a relatively small augmin subcomplex on the MT, as the full-length complex proved a poor structural target. However, by combining our prior knowledge of the structure of the full augmin octamer with the structure of T-IIbonsai on the MT, we can arrive at a model of full-length augmin bound to the MT (Fig. 5a). From this model, we observe that the tip of the augmin complex projects approximately 40 nm from the surface of the MT lattice. The disordered Haus8 MTBR, comprising 154 residues, would, at its full extension, be able to extend 54 nm from the MT lattice surface, although AlphaFold3 models (Supplementary Fig. 3) suggest that it will most commonly sample a region extending 19 nm. Depending where on augmin γ-TuRC binds12,13,17,33, augmin thus may be able to capture both soluble γ-TuRC and growing MT branches at a distance of more than a MT diameter, aiding the complex in its role as a γ-TuRC tether. By modeling multiple augmin complexes bound to the MT, we also note that the MT would quickly become surrounded by a meshwork of augmin complexes. These complexes appear spaced together

too tightly to allow a large molecule such as γ-TuRC—or another MT— to reach down to the MT lattice. This suggests that there may be a tension at the branch site between, on the one hand, recruiting enough augmin to retain weakly-binding soluble γ-TuRC versus, on the other, leaving enough physical space to accommodate other complexes required for branching. Prior biochemical work12 had suggested that the N-terminal MTBR of Haus8 was insufﬁcient to explain the afﬁnity of augmin for the MT lattice. Our work has borne out this hypothesis, ﬁnding that the CH domain of Haus6 substantially enhances the afﬁnity of X. laevis augmin for the MT (Fig. 5b). However, the function of the dual MT binding regions of augmin is not simply to increase augmin’s ability to bind MTs. The bipartite binding site also functions downstream in organizing the MT branch site and controlling the angle at which the new MT emerges. It is relatively straightforward to explain how the Haus6 CH domain accomplishes this. Our structure suggests that the CH domain binds in an ordered manner to the MT lattice. Thus, deletion of an ordered binding site should cause the augmin complex to become more ﬂexibly attached, and would result in the broader distribution of branching angles that we observe (Fig. 5b). However, the role of the Haus8 MTBR is harder to explain. We observe that this region, although disordered in our structure, is critical to keep MT branch angles shallow. Similarly, divergent interphase and mitotic Haus8 MTBRs have been hypothesized to establish cell-cycle-dependent branch angles in vivo in Arabidopsis34. One possible hypothesis for how Haus8 is acting comes from the ability of the Haus8 MTBR to bundle MTs (Supplementary Fig. 12)18. As discussed above, the Haus8 MTBR might bundle MTs either directly, by interacting with tubulin tails on both preexisting and nascent MTs, or else through indirect means, for example reducing electrostatic repulsion by neutralizing the tubulin tails35,36. Regardless of the mechanism, MT bundling, acting on the nascent MT, could lead to a preference for more acute angles; thus, removal of the MT bundler would lead to wider angles, which is in fact what we observe. While our work answers some outstanding questions about the structure and mechanism of MT branching, it also raises others. In particular, the only major component missing from our model of the branch site is now γ-TuRC. Thus, determining where on the augmin complex γ-TuRC binds will complete our structure of the MT branch. Recent work from two groups has provided clues as to augmin’s interaction with γ-TuRC via the NEDD1 adaptor protein. Recent work using A. thaliana augmin and available in preprint from the Al-Bassam group37 shows that the N-terminal WD40 domain of NEDD1 binds to the top of the T-II arch. This binding location is perhaps surprising, as the NEDD1 WD40 domain will, ﬁrst of all, be located too far from the MT surface when docked onto T-II to provide additional MT binding afﬁnity as has been previously hypothesized11. Secondly, as the WD40 domain is connected to the C-terminus of NEDD1, and thus the remainder of γ-TuRC via a ﬂexible linker, this binding interaction will lead to a ﬂexible, not ﬁxed, linkage between augmin and γ-TuRC that seems unlikely to support branching at a ﬁxed angle. A solution to this conundrum is suggested by a second publication from the Pfeffer and Schiebel groups describing the structure of the C-terminus of NEDD1 bound to the base of the γ-TuRC cone38. Using molecular modeling, the authors predict a second, ﬁxed-orientation interaction between the extreme C-terminus of Haus1, representing the farthest tip of T-III, and the C-terminal 4-helix bundle of NEDD1. Thus, it appears that, just as augmin uses both ordered and ﬂexible interactions to bind the MT, it may also use both ordered and ﬂexible interactions to capture and orient γ-TuRC. Prior work11 has also suggested that multiple augmin complexes may be required at a single branch site. In addition to determining how these augmin complexes could recruit one another and their relative orientations, this also begs the question of why multiple copies of augmin are needed. We have previously observed that binding between a single augmin complex and γ-TuRC in solution

is relatively weak13. Therefore, it is possible that the presence of multiple augmin complexes on the MT would strengthen the interaction with γ-TuRC through the effects of avidity. Secondly, our unexpected ﬁnding that the augmin complex prefers the GTPγS lattice, over both the expanded GMPCPP lattice as well as, to a lesser extent, the GDP lattice, is consistent with augmin’s homology to the plus-tip tracker NDC80, but adds a layer of complexity to another open question, the spatiotemporal control of branching. Prior work has suggested that, on dynamic MTs, augmin does not plus track and in fact prefers older MT lattice11. Therefore, although augmin may thermodynamically prefer the structure of “new” MT lattice, it appears that, in practice, binding of augmin to MTs is driven by kinetic effects to prefer the older, although structurally non-ideal, GDP lattice. In this, augmin is similar to TPX2, which, although under some conditions recognizes the GTP or transition state lattice39, in general accumulates on older lattice through a slow (or biphasic) process1,11,30. In line with this, MT branch sites preferentially form on older MT lattice11,31. Thus, within the spindle, it appears that not only MTs themselves exist within a kinetic, not thermodynamic regime, but similarly the factors that control new MT nucleation, at least via the branching process, are themselves controlled by kinetic considerations. In summary, our structural and biochemical work have established the basis for how augmin binds the MT and how augmin binding to the MT helps to orient new MT branches. This work thus advances our understanding of the MT branch site, which is key to generating spindle MTs and to establishing the structure of the spindle itself.

Cryo-EM sample preparation and data collection Guanylyl-α,β-methelynediphosphate (GMPCPP)-stabilized bovine MT seeds were prepared via standard procedures9. In brief, 20 μM bovine tubulin (PurSolutions) was incubated with 1 mM GMPCPP (Jena Biosciences) in 1x BRB80 (80 mM PIPES, pH 6.8, 1 mM EGTA, 1 mM MgCl2) at 37 °C for 1 h. Guanosine 5’-O-[γ-thio]-triphosphate (GTPγS)-stabilized bovine MT seeds were prepared using a protocol adapted from ref. 45. In brief, 36 μM bovine tubulin was incubated with 1 mM GTPγS (Sigma Aldrich) in 1x BRB80 lacking MgCl2 and supplemented with 25% v/v glycerol at 37 °C for 1 h. Seeds were sonicated for 1 min, then 10 μL seeds were added to a fresh 100 μL polymerization reaction containing 33 μM bovine tubulin, 1 mM GTPγS, and 1x BRB80 lacking MgCl2 at 37 °C for 1 h. After the second round of polymerization, seeds were pelleted at room temperature at 17,000 x g for 15 min and resuspended in 1 mM GTPγS and 1x BRB80 lacking MgCl2 at a ﬁnal tubulin concentration of 66 μM. T-IIbonsai was prepared for grid freezing by buffer exchange into cryo-EM buffer (80 mM PIPES pH 6.8, 1 mM EGTA, 1 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT, 0.05% v/v Tween-20) at 4 °C via an 0.5 mL 7 kDa MWCO ZebaSpin desalting column (Thermo Scientiﬁc). After buffer exchange, T-IIbonsai protein was clariﬁed by ultracentrifugation at 279,000 x g at 4 °C for 10 min. Estimation of protein concentration by NanoDrop absorbance at 280 nm suggested a ﬁnal T-IIbonsai concentration of 10 μM. Quantifoil 1.2/1.3 holey carbon grids on a 400-mesh copper support were glow-discharged for 60 s at 10 mA using a Ted Pella easiGlow then loaded onto a Leica GP2 in a humidity chamber pre-incubated at 25 °C and 85% humidity. 3 μL undiluted GMPCPP or GTPγS MT seeds were incubated on grids for 30 s, removed by manual blotting, then 3 μL T-IIbonsai were added and incubated on grids for 30 s, manually blotted, followed by a second application of T-IIbonsai and 30 s incubation. Finally, grids were blotted for 5–7 s by the GP2 and plungefrozen in liquid ethane at −182 °C. Data were collected at the Princeton University Imaging and Analysis Center using ThermoFisher EPU version 2.12.1.2782REL and a G3 Titan Krios equipped with a Gatan BioQuantum energy ﬁlter and Gatan K2 Summit direct electron detector (Supplementary Figs. 6a and 14a). Data collection parameters are summarized in Supplementary Table 1.

Cryo-EM data processing Cryo-EM data processing was performed as previously described in ref. 8 using cryoSPARC version 4.4.046. Motion correction was performed using the patch motion correction algorithm, followed by CTF correction using CTFFind version 447. For the GMPCPP structure, approximately 100 micrographs were manually picked, and templates were generated by 2D classiﬁcation. Templates were then used for autopicking using the ﬁlament tracer utility in cryoSPARC. For the GTPγS structure, microtubules were manually picked as ﬁlaments in Relion 3.1.048, and particles were extracted along the ﬁlament length at a separation of 82.5 Å. Particles were sorted using two rounds of 2D classiﬁcation (Supplementary Figs. 6b, 14b), then 13- and 14- protoﬁlament MTs were sorted by heterogeneous reﬁnement from undecorated references. Alignments for the predominant 14- protoﬁlament class were then further reﬁned using the helical reﬁnement and local reﬁnement routines in cryoSPARC (Supplementary Figs. 6c, 14c). Particles from local reﬁnement were then transferred to Frealign version 949,50 for two rounds of seam searching using the protocol previously outlined8,51. Correctly aligned particles were reimported into cryoSPARC, individually CTF-corrected, and locally reﬁned to produce the C1 map (Supplementary Figs. 6d, 14d). For GMPCPP, symmetry expansion was performed using a helical rise of

8.988 Å, a helical twist of −25.75°, and 11-fold symmetrization (to avoid mis-averaging of α, β-tubulin across the microtubule seam). For GTPγS, symmetry expansion was performed using a helical rise of 9.455 Å, a helical twist of −27.69°, and 11-fold symmetrization The symmetry-expanded data set was further reﬁned using a mask around a tubulin dimer (located at the opposite side of the seam) plus augmin density (Supplementary Figs. 6e, 14e). The GMPCPP map was sharpened using both cryoSPARC “Sharpening Tools” with a B-factor of 60 Å2 and using DeepEMhancer with the tightT setting52. The GTPγS map was ﬁltered using cryoSPARC’s “Local Filter” job.

Model building, reﬁnement, and validation 6DPU, a structure of the porcine 14-protoﬁlament GMPCPP MT lattice28, and chains E-H of 8FCK, a structure of the X. laevis augmin complex14, were used as initial models and rigid-body ﬁt into the symmetry-expanded, sharpened map using UCSF Chimera version 1.13.153. To improve precision of pixel size determination, we empirically determined GMPCPP structure pixel size by calculating the best ﬁt to the tubulin atomic model, slightly rescaling the resulting map from 1.426 to 1.405 Å/pix54. This recalibrated pixel size was used throughout for the GTPγS structure. For the GMPCPP structure, the sequence of 6DPU β-tubulin was mutated to match that of bovine tubulin, and disordered, non-visible regions of augmin were removed from the model in COOT version0.9.8.9355. Reﬁnement was performed using Phenix version 1.17.1-3660 real_space_reﬁne56. For the GTPγS structure, the GMPCPP structure was ﬁt as four rigid bodies—chains A, B, C, and the heterotrimer composed of chains F/G/H—in Chimera, and the GTPγS nucleotide was manually added in COOT. The GMPCPP C1 map is available from the EMDB using accession code EMD-46488, the GMPCPP symmetry-expanded map is available from the EMDB using accession code EMD-46489, and the GTPγS symmetry-expanded map is available from the EMDB using accession code EMD-70593. The GMPCPP model coordinates are available from the PDB using accession code 9D2B and the GTPγS coordinates using accession code 9OLH. Predicted structures of X. laevis augmin T-IIbonsai (tetramer), T-II full-length, and T-IIbonsai (trimer) were generated using AlphaFold357

and are accessible from ModelArchive using the respective accession codes 10.5452/ma-xqslg [https://www.modelarchive.org/doi/10.5452/ ma-xqslg], 10.5452/ma-k2itn [https://www.modelarchive.org/doi/10. 5452/ma-k2itn], and 10.5452/ma-tkb40 [https://www.modelarchive. org/doi/10.5452/ma-tkb40]. Theoretical atomic-coordinate-based maps were calculated using the UCSF Chimera utility molMap at a resolution cut-off of 3.1 Å, the nominal resolution of our structure. Difference maps were calculated between the theoretical map and the sharpened maps using the UCSF Chimera utility vop subtract, followed by a Gaussian volume ﬁlter of 1.0. Buried surface area was calculated using the PISA server58. Map and model ﬁgures were generated using UCSF Chimera version 1.13.153, using the deepEMhancer sharpened map except where indicated, and protein sequence alignments were generated using Clustal Omega59.

Preparation of functionalized coverslips and imaging chambers We used a previously published method to generate functionalized glass coverslips for TIRF imaging43,61,62. Brieﬂy, coverslips were sonicated in 3 M NaOH followed by Piranha solution (2:3 ratio of 30% w/w H2O2 to sulfuric acid). After washing with MilliQ water, we dried and then treated the coverslips with 3-glycidyloxypropyl trimethoxysilane (GOPTS, cat. # 440167, Sigma) at 75 °C for 30 min. Unreacted GOPTS was removed with two sequential acetone washes, and the coverslips were then dried with nitrogen gas. Between sandwiched coverslips, we melted a powder mix of 9 parts HO-PEG-NH2 and 1 part biotin-CONH- PEG-NH2 by weight (cat. #103000–20 and #133000-25-20, Rapp Polymere, Tübingen, Germany) at 75 °C. We pressed out air bubbles and repeated cycles of 75 °C incubation and pressing. After an overnight incubation at 75 °C, the sandwiches were separated and washed in MilliQ water. These were then spun dry in air and stored at 4 °C for up to 1 month. We made imaging chambers by ﬁrst making a channel on a glass slide with double-sided tape. To this channel, we added 2 mg/mL PLL- γ-PEG (SuSOS AG, Dübendorf, Switzerland) in MilliQ water. After a 20 min incubation, the channel was rinsed thoroughly with MilliQ water and dried with nitrogen gas. Using a diamond pen, functionalized coverslips were cut into quarters. Each quarter piece was then added to the double sided tape on the slide with the functionalized surface facing down. Chambers were made fresh on the day of each experiment.

Tubulin labeling and preparation of double cycled GMPCPP-stabilized MTs Bovine brain tubulin was labeled following prior methods9. Using Alexa568-NHS ester (Invitrogen; A20003) yielded 36–40% labeling efﬁciency. Double cycled GMPCPP-stabilized MTs were made as previously described (42, 63). Brieﬂy, 18 μM unlabeled bovine tubulin supplemented with 1 μM Alexa568 labeled tubulin and 1 μM biotinylated tubulin was polymerized in BRB80 buffer (80 mM PIPES, pH 6.8, 1 mM EGTA, and 1 mM MgCl2) in the presence of 1 mM GMPCPP for 1 h at 37 °C. After 1 h, the MT seed mixture was centrifuged at 17,000 x g at room temperature for 15 min. The remaining pellet was then resuspended in cold BRB80 and left on ice to depolymerize for 20 min, followed by a second round of polymerization with 1 mM GMPCPP for 1 h at 37 °C. After 1 h, the mixture was centrifuged again at 17,000 x g at room temperature for 15 min. The supernatant was removed, and the

pellet was resuspended in warm BRB80 and snap frozen in 1 μL aliquots and stored at −80 °C for later use.

Preparation of subtilisin-cleaved, GMPCPP MT seeds Single cycled, GMPCPP-stabilized MT seeds were ﬁrst prepared. Brieﬂy, 18 μM unlabeled bovine tubulin supplemented with 1 μM Alexa568 labeled tubulin and 1 μM biotinylated tubulin was polymerized in BRB80 buffer (80 mM PIPES, pH 6.8, 1 mM EGTA, and 1 mM MgCl2) in the presence of 1 mM GMPCPP for 1 h at 37 °C. After 1 h, the MT seed mixture was centrifuged at 17,000 x g at room temperature for 15 min. The supernatant was removed and the pellet was resuspended in warm BRB80 supplemented with 1 mM GMPCPP. The MTs were then incubated with 100 ug/ml Subtilisin A, and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. 2 mM PMSF was then added to quench the reaction, and the seeds were spun down at 17,000 × g at room temperature for 15 min. The supernatant was removed, and the pellet was washed one time with BRB80 to remove any additional Subtilisin A. The ﬁnal pellet was resuspended in warm BRB80, and used immediately for TIRF microscopy experiments.

Preparation of dual-labeled MT seeds To prepare dual-labeled GMPCPP-GTPγS MT seeds, we modiﬁed a previously established protocol for growing GTPγS MTs from GMPCPP templates28. 20 μM bovine brain tubulin with 10% Atto 647 N (ATTO- TEC Gmbh) labeled tubulin and 10% biotinylated tubulin were incubated on ice for 5 min then polymerized in the presence of 1 mM GMPCPP at 37 °C for 1 h in BRB80. The seeds were pelleted by centrifugation at 17,000 ×g at room temperature for 15 min, then resuspended in 10% Alexa568 labeled 50 μM tubulin in modiﬁed BRB80 buffer containing 0.2 mM MgCl2 and 1 mM guanosine 5’-O-[γ-thio]triphosphate (GTPγS) (pre-incubated on ice for 5 min). The mixture was then polymerized for 1 h at 37 °C. These seeds were pelleted again by the same means and resuspended in 0.2 mM MgCl2 BRB80 supplemented with 1 mM DTT. To prepare a 1:1 mixture of labeled GTPγS and GDP seeds, we modiﬁed the above protocol to produce GMPCPP-Atto-647N GTPγS seeds by omitting ﬂuorescently labeled tubulin from the ﬁrst GMPCPP polymerization step and substituting 10% Atto-647N-labeled tubulin for Alexa568-labeled tubulin in the second GTPγS polymerization step. We produced GMPCPP-capped Alexa568-labeled GDP seeds in the following way. 20 μM bovine brain tubulin with 10% Alexa568-labeled tubulin and 10% biotinylated tubulin in BRB80 supplemented with 15% v/v glycerol were incubated on ice for 5 min then polymerized in the presence of 1 mM GTP at 37 °C for 45 min. The seeds were pelleted by centrifugation at 17,000 × g at room temperature for 15 min, then resuspended in 1 μM tubulin in BRB80 buffer containing 1 mM GMPCPP and 15% v/v glycerol, which had been preincubated on ice for 5 min. The second polymerization step was then performed for 45 min at 37 °C. Seeds were again pelleted as above and resuspended in room temperature 0.2 mM MgCl2 BRB80. For attachment, GMPCPP-GTPγS and GDP-GMPCPP seeds were diluted and mixed using a ﬁnal ratio of 1 part GMPCPP-GTPγS, 1 part GDP-GMPCPP, and 300 parts 0.2 mM MgCl2 BRB80.

Attachment of stabilized MTs to PEGfunctionalized coverslips Flow chambers were incubated with 5% v/v Pluronic F-127 in water (Invitrogen; catalog no.: P6866) for 5 min at room temperature and then washed with assay buffer (BRB80; 5 mM BME, 0.075% w/v methylcellulose, 1% w/v glucose, 0.02% v/v Brij-35 [Thermo Scientiﬁc; catalog no.: 20150]) supplemented with 50 μg/mL κ-casein. Flow chambers were then incubated with an assay buffer containing 50 μg/ mL NeutrAvidin (Invitrogen; catalog no.: A2666) for 2 min on a metal block on ice and subsequently washed with BRB80. Binding of proteins to GMPCPP MT seeds Before initiating branching MT nucleation, TPX2 (10 nM), augmin constructs (~75 nM), and y-TuRC (~75 nM) were sequentially ﬂowed into the ﬂow chambers containing attached GMPCPP-stabilized MT seeds attached to the surface. TPX2 was added at a concentration of 10 nM, below the phase boundary, to prevent formation of condensates. All proteins were diluted into CSF-XB buffer with 8% w/v sucrose. Proteins were incubated for 5 min at room temperature. Unbound proteins were removed with additional BRB80 washes prior to incubation of the next protein. Additionally, prior to each protein incubation, the ﬂow chamber was washed with a blocking buffer containing 1 mg/mL κ-casein. For experiments testing the binding of augmin constructs to GMPCPP seeds without TPX2 present (as in Fig. 2), all augmin constructs were diluted directly into a CSF-XB-based imaging buffer containing oxygen scavengers and imaged directly after a 10 min incubation without washing the channels.

MT bundling experiments To determine if a MAP was capable of bundling two MTs, biotinylated, Alexa647 GMPCPP-stabilized MT seeds were ﬁrst bound to a glass coverslip asdescribed in the previous section. Next, augmin constructs were mixed with Alexa568 GMPCPP-stabilized MT seeds and immediately ﬂowed into the channel. This mixture was incubated for 10 min before washing with BRB80 and imaging via TIRF. The augmin construct was considered able to bundle if the two colors of MT seeds (Alexa568, Alexa647) co-localized with one another along with the GFP-labeled augmin.

Binding of proteins to dual-labeled MT seeds and analysis Dual-labeled seeds were attached to PEG-functionalized coverslips (as above), and EB1, TPX2, and augmin octamer imaging mixtures were prepared in a 5% w/v sucrose CSF-XB-based imaging buffer as described above. All reactions were imaged within 10 min. 3 × 3 arrays were imaged using a Nikon Ti-E inverted stand (RRID:SCR_021242) with an Apo TIRF 100 x oil objective (NA = 1.49) and an Andor iXon DU-897 EM- CCD camera with EM gain set to 300. Microscopy data were processed using a custom macro in FIJI/ImageJ. Background subtraction was performed using the Subtract Background command on the MAP channel. MT seeds were segmented into regions of interest by automatically thresholding the GMPCPP, GTPγS, and/or GDP channels as applicable using the Otsu method63 and selecting particles the “Analyze Particles” function with minimum 1.0 μm2 area and a circularity range of 0.0–0.5. Average MAP ﬂuorescent signals per pixel were calculated for each MT.

MT nucleation assays on PEG-functionalized surfaces For branching MT nucleation reactions in vitro, BFP-TPX2 (10 nM), GFP-augmin ( ~ 75 nM) and γ-TuRC ( ~ 75 nM) were added sequentially to the chamber containing attached GMPCPP-stabilized MTs and incubated for 5 min at room temperature. Unbound proteins were removed by additional BRB80 washes, followed by washes with 1 mg/ mL κ-casein in BRB80. The ﬁnal assay mixture was ﬂowed into the chambers: 80 mM PIPES, pH 6.8, 30 mM KCl, 1 mM EGTA, 1 mM MgCl2, 1 mM GTP, 5 mM BME, 0.075% w/v methylcellulose (4000 cP), 1% w/v glucose, 0.02% v/v Brij-35, 250 nM glucose oxidase, 64 nM catalase, 1 mg/mL BSA, 19 μM unlabeled bovine tubulin and 1 μM Cy5-labeled bovine tubulin. Before use, all proteins were pre-cleared of aggregates via ultracentrifugation at 346,000 × g for 15 min in a TLA100 rotor in an Optima MAX-XP ultracentrifuge at 4 °C.

TIRF imaging and image analysis Total internal reﬂection ﬂuorescence (TIRF) microscopy was performed with a Nikon TiE microscope using a 100 × 1.49 NA objective. Andor Zyla sCMOS camera was used for acquisition, with a ﬁeld of view of 165.1 × 139.3 µm. 2 × 2 binned, multi-color images were acquired using NIS-Elements version 5.02.01-Build 1270 (Nikon). All adjustable imaging parameters (exposure time, laser intensity, and TIRF angle) were kept the same within experiments. For MT nucleation assays in vitro, the TIRF objective was warmed to 33 °C using an objective heater (Bioptechs, 150819–13). For all time-lapse imaging, one multi-color image was taken at the beginning of the experiment followed by collection of time-lapse images on the 647 nm channel every 2 s for 10 min. After the time lapse was collected, another multi-color image was taken. For still images of augmin binding and branched MT nucleation experiments, an additional 15–30 multi-color images were collected. Brightness and contrast were optimized individually for display. Images used for the quantiﬁcation of MT binding were analyzed using FIJI/ImageJ. Background subtraction was performed using the Subtract Background command on the MAP channel. To segment MTs, the tubulin signal was ﬁrst thresholded via the Otsu method. MTs were isolated from the mask by setting the minimum particle area as 1 or 2 μm2. Average ﬂuorescent signals per pixel, for the MT or for bound proteins, were calculated for each MT. The average intensity from the reverse mask of the entire ﬁeld of view was subtracted from the average intensity on each MT. For branching MT nucleation experiments in vitro, MTs were counted manually using time-lapse experiments, and multiple aspects of the data were taken into account to exclude MTs of ambiguous origin. In the case where branched MTs were quantiﬁed from still images, the MTs were counted manually and only included in the analysis if there was a clear distinction between the plus and minus end of the MT. Additionally, branched MTs were excluded from analysis if two microtubule seeds were close to each other on the glass coverslip, and the origin of the daughter MT was ambiguous in a still image. Branched MTs were also excluded if there was a possibility of what we term a crossing event, where a spontaneously nucleated MT could be above the immobilized seed. In the case that the origin of the branched MT was still ambiguous, kymographs were prepared from the live movies to detect which MTs were true branches vs. spontaneously nucleated (Supplementary Fig. 22). Branch angles were measured manually using FIJI/ImageJ. For nearly parallel branch angles of <5 degrees, kymographs were made of the MT plus ends to show that a second MT was growing in addition to the polymerizing MT end (Supplementary Fig. 19, Supplementary Movie 6). To quantify parallel branch angles in the still images, the mean intensity of the plus end was quantiﬁed to show that the intensity was twice of that expected if there was only a single MT polymerizing from the plus end (Supplementary Fig. 20). The branch angle distributions were plotted as histograms in Prism.

# Conformational states of the microtubule nucleator, the γ-tubulin ring complex

**Authors:** Brianna Romer; Sophie M Travis; Brian P Mahon; Collin T McManus; Philip D Jeffrey; Nicolas Coudray; Rishwanth Raghu; Michael J Rale; Ellen D Zhong; Gira Bhabha; Sabine Petry

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA | 2Present address: Molecular Structure and Design, Bristol Myers Squibb, Princeton, NJ, USA | 3Department of Cell Biology, NYU School of Medicine, New York City, NY, USA | 4Applied Bioinformatics Laboratories, NYU School of Medicine, New York, NY, USA | 5Department of Computer Science, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA | 6Present address: Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Microtubules (MTs) perform essential functions in the cell, and it is critical that they are made at the correct cellular location and cell cycle stage. This nucleation process is catalyzed by the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC), a cone-shaped protein complex composed of over 30 subunits. Despite recent insight into the structure of vertebrate γ-TuRC, which shows that its diameter is wider than that of a MT, and that it exhibits little of the symmetry expected for an ideal MT template, the question of how γ-TuRC achieves MT nucleation remains open. Here, we utilized single particle cryo-EM to identify two conformations of γ-TuRC. The helix composed of 14 γ-tubulins at the top of the γ-TuRC cone undergoes substantial deformation, which is predominantly driven by bending of the hinge between the GRIP1 and GRIP2 domains of the γ-tubulin complex proteins. However, surprisingly, this deformation does not remove the inherent asymmetry of γ-TuRC. To further investigate the role of γ-TuRC conformational change, we used cryo electron-tomography (cryo-ET) to obtain a 3D reconstruction of γ-TuRC bound to a nucleated MT, providing insight into the post-nucleation state. Rigid-body fitting of our cryo-EM structures into this reconstruction suggests that the MT lattice is nucleated by spokes 2 through 14 of the γ-tubulin helix, which entails spokes 13 and 14 becoming more structured than what is observed in apo γ-TuRC. Together, our results allow us to propose a model for conformational changes in γ-TuRC and how these may facilitate MT formation in a cell.

## INTRODUCTION

Microtubules (MTs) are dynamic polymers that are formed by head-to-tail protofilaments of α/β-tubulin dimers assembled into a hollow cylinder. MTs are found in all eukaryotes and function in many diverse and essential cellular processes, such as organelle positioning, intracellular transport, and, during cell division, the segregation of chromosomes. For all these critical functions, it is imperative that MTs are generated, or nucleated, at the correct place and time. While spontaneous nucleation of MTs can be driven by high concentrations of tubulin dimers in vitro, nucleation of new MTs in the cell is tightly controlled and requires catalysis1, 2. Essential for cellular MT nucleation is the universal MT template, a 2.2 MDa complex known as the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC)3, 4.

γ-TuRC was first discovered and characterized in Xenopus laevis meiotic egg extract5, where it was shown to form a cone-shaped structure capable of both nucleating and capping MTs. However, much of the initial work on γ-TuRC focused on the more biochemically and structurally tractable Saccharomyces cerevisiae complex. In the cytoplasm, yeast γ-TuRC exists as the so-called γ-tubulin small complex (γ-TuSC), a ‘V’-shaped hetero-tetramer composed of two γ-tubulin molecules bound to the spoke proteins Spc97 and Spc986, 7. When recruited to the MT-nucleating spindle pole body by Spc110, seven γ-TuSCs assemble into a cone topped by a helix of 14 γ-tubulins8. This γ-tubulin helix can nucleate MTs in vitro and somewhat mimics the geometry of a 13-protofilament MT, albeit with a wider diameter. Strikingly, artificially “closing” yeast γ-TuRC to match the diameter of a MT—by introducing disulfide-based crosslinks into γ-tubulin—enhances the complex’s nucleation activity three-fold9. This result thus prompted the hypothesis that, in the cell, γ-TuRC would change conformation and “close” to a symmetric, MT-like active state during the nucleation reaction.

Recent advances in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) have led to the determination of the structure of vertebrate γ-TuRC10, 11, 12. Like yeast γ-TuRC, vertebrate γ-TuRC is roughly cone-shaped, topped by a 14 γ-tubulin helix. However, vertebrate γ-TuRC contains complexity and asymmetry not present in yeast γ-TuRC. At spoke positions 9–12, GCP2 and GCP3 (the vertebrate orthologs of Spc97 and Spc98, respectively), are replaced by their paralogs GCP4, GCP5, and GCP6. This substitution has been previously reported to cause this region of the γ-tubulin helix to form a less symmetric structure than the γ-TuSC spokes10 and thus a poorer match to the highly symmetric MT helix. Furthermore, the base of the cone is stabilized by monomeric actin, the N-termini of GCP3 and GCP6, and small MZT proteins13, 14. Likely due to these additional, stabilizing interactions, vertebrate γ-TuRC remains assembled in the cytoplasm10, 11, 12, 14, and CDK5RAP2, the vertebrate homolog of Spc110, promotes only γ-TuRC recruitment and activation, not assembly15, 16. However, most importantly, vertebrate γ-TuRC also appears to exist predominantly in an inactive, “open” state10, 11. How, and even if, vertebrate γ-TuRC changes conformation to an activated, nucleation-competent state remains unclear.

In this work, we have determined structures of two conformations of X. laevis γ-TuRC, allowing us to characterize possible conformations of γ-TuRC that may underlie nucleation. We find that the γ-tubulin helix at the top of the γ-TuRC cone is able to undergo substantial deformation due to bending at an internal hinge within individual spokes. However, interestingly, this deformation does not resolve the intrinsic asymmetry observed in vertebrate γ-TuRC. In addition, we have obtained a 3D reconstruction of the γ-TuRC capped MT via cryo-electron tomography, allowing us to visualize a low-resolution envelope of the complex. Our structures combined with the cryo-ET data allow us to propose a model for how conformational changes within γ-TuRC may lead to the generation of MTs.

## RESULTS

### Activity of purified Xenopus laevis γ-TuRC

In order to investigate the structure of γ-TuRC, we obtained γ-TuRC from Xenopus laevis meiotic egg extract using an endogenous purification strategy15, which takes advantage of the high-affinity interaction between γ-TuRC and a fragment of CDK5RAP2 known the γ-TuNA (γ-TuRC nucleation activator). Next, we used a single-molecule MT nucleation assay to assess the activity of our purified γ-TuRC12, 15. Coverslips were coated with biotinylated γ-TuRC, then incubated with a MT nucleation mixture containing fluorescently labeled tubulin and either 6 μM γ-TuNA or buffer. MT nucleation from the immobilized γ-TuRC molecules was then monitored via total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy. Consistent with previously published results, we found that our purified γ-TuRC was capable of nucleating MTs (Figure 1a). Additionally, when reactions were supplemented with exogenous γ-TuNA activator, the rate of MT nucleation increased 6.7-fold (Figure 1b)15, while other reaction parameters remained unchanged (Supplementary Figure 1a,b). Taken together, these results confirmed the suitability of our purified γ-TuRC for structural studies.

### Cryo-EM reconstruction of Xenopus laevis γ-TuRC

Next, we proceeded to structural determination of γ-TuRC. Because we wanted γ-TuRC to be in its most active state, we adapted the conditions used for MT nucleation, supplementing the γ-TuRC sample with 6 μM γ-TuNA. We then collected a large single-particle cryo-EM dataset and performed extensive 3D classification and refinement in cryoSPARC17 (Supplementary Table 1, Supplementary Figure 2 and 3), resulting in an cryo-EM density map of γ-TuRC at a global resolution of 3.1 Å (Figure 1c, Supplementary Figure 4). In line with previous cryo-EM analysis of γ-TuRC10, 11, 12, different regions of the complex displayed substantially different local resolution estimates. The base of the γ-TuRC cone reached the highest resolutions, and the top of the cone, corresponding to the γ-tubulin helix, had a lower average resolution (Figure 1c,d). Spokes 13–14 had the lowest resolution of the entire complex, suggesting substantial conformational and/or compositional heterogeneity.

### γ-TuRC undergoes substantial molecular motion

To examine whether and how particle heterogeneity was contributing to regions of low resolution in our map, we first used 3D variability analysis (3DVA)18, a method for calculating the principal components (PCs) of variability from a consensus cryo-EM structure. We analyzed the three largest principal components of variability (Supplementary Videos 1–3), which encompassed clamshell-like motions hinging at different locations around the γ-tubulin helix. Across all these principal components of variability, the base of the γ-TuRC cone moves the least, whereas top, corresponding to the γ-tubulin helix, has the most dramatic motions. From this analysis, we found that γ-TuRC appears to undergo a complex series of conformational changes, and, moreover, that these motions entail substantial re-arrangement of the γ-tubulin helix.

To ensure that we were capturing the full range of conformational change, and as a complementary analysis, we explored conformational variability within our data using cryoDRGN19, a deep learning algorithm that can extract complex, non-linear molecular motions from single-particle cryo-EM data. CryoDRGN found two major clusters representing compositional and conformational heterogeneity: an outlier cluster (top, gray) that lacked density for spokes 13 and 14, thus representing incomplete complexes, and a second cluster corresponding to intact γ-TuRC particles (Figure 1e, Supplementary Video 4). Reconstructions sampled from the second, intact particle cluster exhibited conformational motions identical to the largest component of variability from 3DVA, and the conformational extremes from 3DVA could be visualized in the space as distinct regions of the latent space (Figure 1f).

### Molecular models of two major γ-TuRC conformations

To understand the molecular basis of this conformational change in γ-TuRC, we reconstructed volumes corresponding to the two conformational extremes of the bottom, intact particle cluster, which we will refer to as Class 1 and Class 2 (Figure 1c, Supplementary Video 5), and obtained refined density maps of similar quality for these two classes (Supplementary Figure 5–7). Next, we proceeded to build molecular models for both classes, starting from previously published structures10, 11, 13, 14 and performed model refinement (Table 1).

Based on the resolution of our Class 1 and Class 2 maps, we were able to model regions that have thus far remained unresolved, adding to the completeness of prior γ-TuRC models. We observed peptide density on spokes 1 and 2 in the γ-TuRC lumen that was consistent in sequence with the N-terminus of GCP6 (Supplementary Figure 8a). This result suggests an even greater role of GCP6 in γ-TuRC assembly than previously reported14, as GCP6 comes into contact with every spoke in γ-TuRC except for spoke 14. We additionally scrutinized the outside surface of γ-TuRC for density corresponding to the γ-TuNA activating peptide. The first potential location for γ-TuNA reported was an extended peptide region termed the “staple” that was found in human γ-TuRC between each GCP2 and GCP3 of a γ-TuSC pair10. This density was also visible in our structure; however, in agreement with the more recent structure of recombinant human γ-TuRC 14, we interpreted this region as an N-terminal stretch of GCP2 (Supplementary Figure 8b). An updated model of human γ-TuRC bound to γ-TuNA13 instead attributed coiled-coil density on the outside of spoke 13 to the γ-TuNA dimer, held in place by the N-terminus of the spoke 13 GCP2 bound to MZT2. Despite extensive refinement of spoke 13, in neither the Class 1 nor the Class 2 map could we observe density consistent with γ-TuNA nor the GCP2/MZT2 module on that spoke (Supplementary Figure 8c). We also did not observe density consistent with γ-TuNA at any previously unattributed position. We suspect the absence of clear γ-TuNA density may be attributed to a difference in binding conditions or else to an intrinsic difference in binding affinity and/or location between human and Xenopus γ-TuRC.

### Global rearrangement of γ-tubulin subunits during conformational change

The prevailing model of γ-TuRC activation predicts that γ-TuRC will be able to change conformation to better match the geometry of a MT. To date in the field, this global conformational change has been described in terms of changes in the diameter of the γ-tubulin helix10, 11. However, our analysis was confounded when we used this metric to compare our two conformations, as we found that the radius to the helical axis varied substantially depending on which spoke of the ring we examined (Figure 2a,b). At certain locations within the ring, centered on spokes 1 and 10, the radius was the narrowest and approached MT radius (Figure 2b, dashed line); however, the ring buckled out at spokes 7–8 for Class 1, 5–6 for Class 2, and 13–14 for both classes. In addition, measuring radius alone did not allow us to capture other ways that the γ-tubulin helix might change conformation, such as alterations in helical pitch or helical rise (Figure 2c). Thus, we developed a new and more complete approach to capture γ-tubulin displacement. First, we extracted the displacement vector required to move each γ-tubulin from its position in Class 1 to its position in Class 2 (Figure 2c,d). Then, we extracted three orthogonal directions of motion—left/right, down/up, and in/out—that describe how each γ-tubulin moves in the frame of reference of the γ-tubulin helix (Figure 2d).

By comparing all three types of motion across all 14 tubulins of the ring, a few major trends emerge (Figure 2e). First, most of the displacement occurs in the left/right and in/out directions, and very little displacement of γ-tubulin up or down in the plane of the helix is observed. Secondly, displacement in these two orthogonal directions is coupled. Displacement into the ring (ring closure, dashed line in Figure 2e) likely results in more crowding in the γ-TuRC lumen, and thus is generally coupled with a clockwise rotation towards spoke 14 (unspooling of the γ-tubulin helix, solid line in Figure 2e). To counteract this global deformation, displacement out of the ring (ring opening, dashed line) is, conversely, coupled with a counterclockwise rotation towards spoke 1 (respooling of the γ-tubulin helix, solid line). Many parts of the ring, most notably spokes 9–12, appear to be relatively static between the two conformations (Supplementary Figure 9), and the largest conformational difference between Class 1 and Class 2 appeared to be an exchange in two γ-TuSCs—in Class 1, the spoke 5–6 γ-TuSC leans into the ring and the spoke 7–8 γ-TuSC leans out, whereas in Class 2, the spoke 5–6 γ-TuSC now leans out of the ring and the spoke 7–8 γ-TuSC leans in. In conclusion, any “closure” of the γ-tubulin helix in a subset of spokes appears to be coupled with an equivalent “opening” elsewhere in the ring.

### Local asymmetry of the γ-tubulin helix is preserved during conformational change

For activated γ-TuRC to become a more perfect MT template, the γ-tubulin helix will need to match the geometry of the MT not only in terms of global parameters—for example, diameter—but also locally. In particular, the spacing between adjacent γ-tubulins will need to match the spacing between MT protofilaments. Therefore, we measured the distance between γ-tubulin subunits in adjacent spokes and compared with the distance between protofilaments in the MT helix (Figure 3a). In contrast to the global displacement of γ-tubulins of up to 10–15 Å between Class 1 and Class 2 described above (Figure 2e), the two classes had similar separation between adjacent γ-tubulins (Figure 3b, Supplementary Figure 10a). The largest distance change, 3 Å, was located between spokes 12 and 13; however, due to the low local resolution in this region, we cannot conclude that this change reflects a true difference between the two classes.

While any difference between Class 1 and Class 2 inter-γ-tubulin distances was generally less than 1 Å, the variation in distance between γ-tubulins of adjacent spokes around the ring was much more pronounced, up to 6 Å, independent of the class (Figure 3b). In the region of γ-TuRC composed of γ-TuSCs, γ-tubulin distances alternate: within a γ-TuSC pair (e.g. spoke 1 to 2) γ-tubulins are closely spaced, whereas between γ-TuSCs (e.g. spoke 2 to 3), γ-tubulins are spaced further apart (as also noted in 11). However, where GCP4/5/4/6 substitutes for γ-TuSCs, this pattern is broken, and all γ-tubulins are separated by the same, larger spacing (Figure 3b).

We next wanted to understand how γ-tubulin spacing could relate to ring closure; therefore, we compared these distances to those found between the protofilaments of a MT (dashed line in Figure 3b). In the MT, tubulin dimers are separated by 54.2 Å (PDB accession 7SJ720), and, surprisingly, this distance is most consistent with the further apart, or more open distances in γ-TuRC (Figure 3b). This is also the distance found between γ-tubulins in the “closed” disulfide-linked active yeast γ-TuRC (PDB accession 7M2W21). Therefore, the most “closed,” or closest, γ-tubulin distances within vertebrate γ-TuRC deviate the most from MT geometry and appear to be too closely spaced to properly nucleate a MT.

Is γ-TuRC likely to be able to change conformations to “open” its γ-TuSC pairs to a MT-like geometry? To answer this question, we investigated the intermolecular contacts that drive association of adjacent γ-TuRC spokes. By comparing buried surface area (BSA) (Figure 3c), we found that BSA changed little between Class 1 and Class 2, but that spokes that comprised a γ-TuSC pair had greater BSA than other spoke pairs (Figure 3d, Supplementary Figure 10b–d). This increase in surface area results both from increased contact between γ-tubulins, as well as from the presence of the staple peptide sandwiched between GCP2 and GCP3, and it suggests that each γ-TuSC is a relatively rigid, autonomous unit. This result is in line with prior work demonstrating that pre-assembled γ-TuSC units load onto the assembling γ-TuRC11, 14; however, it also suggests that separating the γ-tubulins of a vertebrate γ-TuSC to resemble the MT would be energetically unfavorable.

### Role of GCPs in positioning the γ-tubulin helix

If neither the distances between γ-tubulins nor the areas buried between adjacent spokes change substantially between Class 1 and Class 2, what then leads to the rearrangement we observe within the γ-tubulin helix? The most substantial inter-spoke contacts in γ-TuRC are found at the base of the cone, within the GRIP1 domain of the GCPs, and, in contrast, GRIP2 and γ-tubulin generate relatively minor and variable contact surfaces. Therefore, we wondered whether a hinge movement between the two GRIP domains of each spoke could lead to γ-tubulin repositioning (Figure 3e). When we measured the angle between GRIPs, we found that it varied up to 7° depending on the spoke measured and up to 4° between Class 1 and Class 2 (Figure 3f). As previously described, the largest conformational changes between Class 1 and Class 2 represent a “flip-flop” exchange of spokes 5–6 and spokes 7–8 (Figure 2b,e), and these spokes also represent the largest changes in GRIP angle between Class 1 and Class 2 (Figure 3f). More specifically, increase in the angle between GRIP1 and GRIP2 correlates with displacement of a spoke out of the ring. Consistent with this general pattern, the GRIP1/2 angle of spokes 5–6 is greater in Class 2 than Class 1 (Figure 3f), and in Class 2 these spokes lean out of the ring in comparison with Class 1. The opposite pattern is observed for spoke 7–8, which lean into the ring in Class 2 when compared with Class 1. Thus, bending of the GRIP1/2 hinge appears to be linked to the conformational change observed between the two γ-TuRC classes. In contrast to γ-tubulin distances, we find that the range of angles adopted by vertebrate GRIPs is similar to that found in yeast γ-TuRC, with the exception of GCP411. However, GRIP angles are far more asymmetric around the vertebrate ring than are their yeast counterparts.

### Cryo-ET of a γ-TuRC nucleated and capped MT

Up to this point, we have examined spontaneous conformational change within γ-TuRC, which may not correlate directly with the changes that occur during MT nucleation. To gain a better understanding of MT nucleation, we turned to cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), with the goal of studying γ-TuRC in complex with MTs. Because MT nucleation and MT polymerization compete for the same starting material (namely, soluble tubulin dimers), in order to maximize MT nucleation complexes, we needed to also suppress MT polymerization. To accomplish this task, an engineered MT capping protein, known as DARPin TM-322, 23, was titrated into the reaction at a concentration that restricts MT length to about 1 μm (Figure 4a, Supplementary Figure 11). After MTs capped with γ-TuRC were nucleated in the presence of DARPin TM-3 and the MT stabilizer paclitaxel, 105 tilt series were collected and reconstructed into tomograms (Supplementary Table 1). In the resulting tomograms, we were able to easily differentiate γ-TuRC capped MTs from open MT ends (Figure 4b).
